Women in Congress: Despite the fact that women represent about 50% of the US population, only 27% of congresspeople are women.

No Female US President: One of the starkest representations of the glass ceiling is that there has never been a female president of the United States, despite the fact many women have aspired to high office and tried to work their way up in the man's world of politics. The closest female to the office was Hillary Clinton, who said she wanted to shatter the "highest, hardest glass ceiling."

Obama as First Black Presidents: Despite the fact that 13% of the US population is black, there has only ever been one black president.

Lack of Female CEOs: Only 24 of the top 500 companies are run by women, demonstrating the difficulties women face in climbing the corporate ladder.

Female Head Teachers: It is only recently that women have started to occupy high-up positions within organizations, demonstrating cracks in the glass ceiling. But even in feminized professions, the higher-up posts are proportionally more male. For example, despite 74% of teachers being women, they represent 65% of head teacher positions in the UK.

Female Vice Presidents: Just as there has been a lack of female presidents, we can see that there is also a historical lack of female vice presidents. Kamala Harris was the first.

Causes of the Glass Ceiling

Discrimination against potential mothers: Women who are entering an age where they may have children may not be offered promotions at the workplace, while paternity is not contemplated amongst men of the same birth cohort.

People from ethnic minority backgrounds are sometimes left behind in their careers due to discriminatory hiring practices in the workplace.

Gender stereotypes: Sexist stereotypes, for example, thinking of women as more emotional and unable to fulfill leadership roles, contribute to the perpetuation of the glass ceiling

Exclusion from informal networks: Women are often locked out from "informal networks", for example, going for afterwork drinks with managers, which puts them at a disadvantage in career advancement.

The gay glass ceiling: Homosexual men's careers also feel the impact of glass ceilings as research has found they are often concentrated in low-level managerial positions, not at the top (Aksoy et al., 2019).

Discrimination against gay people: People with disabilities have been found to have difficulties both entering the job market and then advancing in their careers once they have secured a job.

Intersectional discrimination: Ethnic minority women often suffer double discrimination when it comes to workplace promotion, and may find it harder to shatter the glass ceiling.

Unnoticed effort: Women trying harder at their job by, for example, trying to make their ideas stand up as a meeting, is also an example of the effects of the glass ceiling (Chisholm-Burns et al., 2017).

Motherhood as a barrier: Motherhood often penalizes women when it comes to advancing in their careers, while it is not the same for fathers, who keep on climbing their professional career.

Attempts to Address the Glass Ceiling

The debate over how to address the glass ceiling generally revolves around how aggressively governments or corporations should intervene to achieve equality of representation.

Below are some common solutions and the arguments for and against each.

1. Affirmative Action

Affirmative action refers to policies to intentionally hire or preference underrepresented groups. On a macro scale, this gets underrepresented people into positions of power and helps achieve political and sociological goals.

However, critics argue that it restrains hiring committees and may lead to worse performance. If the best candidate is a male, for example, then the company should have the freedom to choose the male candidate.

Furthermore, this policy may instill a sense that women only got the job because of their gender identity. To challenge this point, however, we could argue that historically men have only gotten leadership positions because of their gender identities, too.

2. Quotas

Like affirmative action, quotas are used to put pressure on an organization to hire underrepresented groups.

An example of a quota might be "to ensure 60% of new hires are women." This allows a hiring committee to split the hiring pool – so, for example, they can hire 4 men and 6 women in a hiring round when they hire 10 people.

In politics, it might mean that a party will decide that 50% of their candidates will be women in the next election. one complaint about this, however, has been that the parties will run women in regions where they will definitely lose, and run men in the more desirable or competitive races, leading to more men getting elected in the end.

3. Scholarships and Internships

A less coercive policy is to offer scholarships and internships to underrepresented groups.

This approach aims to give people from underrepresented groups the best chance possible to succeed in interviews, without actually forcing the hand of the interviewers.

The criticism of this policy is that it doesn't do anything to tangibly address implicit biases that hiring committees have that will lead them to hiring male or racial majority candidates, even if the female or minority candidates are better.

Research conducted in the UK showed that gay men were more likely to be in managerial positions or have supervisory responsibilities than heterosexual similar men (Giray Aksoy et al., 2019).

However, a more detailed look showed that the managerial positions held were at the lower level of the scale. The highest level managerial positions were harder to reach for gay men than otherwise similar heterosexual men.

For lesbians, the results were similar. While compared to heterosexual women, lesbians were more likely to have managerial authority, but like gay men, they were less likely to be in the highest managerial or supervisory roles.

There was evidence related to discriminatory practices and also of intersectionality: what has been called the "gay glass ceiling effect" was stronger for ethnic minorities than for whites.

3. Disability Research

The glass ceiling, its obstacles, and barriers also affect the work life of people living with disabilities (Nario-Redmond, 2019). A mix of organizational and attitudinal barriers makes it harder for people with disabilities to advance in their careers.

Research has shown that people with disabilities are still concentrated and over-represented in lower-paid service jobs (Nario-Redmond, 2019; Wilson-Kovacsa et al., 2008). However, in higher-paid managerial and professional positions, they are under-represented.

This situation happens despite the fact that people with disabilities often have equivalent qualifications and work experience as non-disabled work colleagues. And still, they have less opportunities of upward mobility, meaning that the glass ceiling is on full force.

4. Race and Ethnicity Research

Ethnic and racial minorities also see their career advancement halted by the existence of a glass ceiling (Gee & Peck, 2018).

Studies from the US show, for example, that race is a stronger factor than gender in determining a person's chances of being promoted or holding higher managerial positions (Gee & Peck, 2018). This points at the importance of intersectionality when thinking about the glass ceiling (Bloch et al., 2020).

Also, not all ethnic minorities have the same trajectories. In the US context Asians, for example, may be more likely to be hired, but the least likely to be promoted. This has come to be called "the bamboo ceiling" (Yu, 2020).

5. The Maternal Wall Research

Women of childbearing age, pregnant women and those with children are all subjected to the effects of the glass ceiling (Williams, 2015).

Motherhood, or its prospect, seems to be a factor in determining women's career projections and advancements. Fatherhood, however, does not affect men's professional lives in the same manner, pointing at gender bias and inequality.

What has come to be called the "maternal wall", is a situation in which women do not even reach the "glass ceiling" due to a type of gender bias related to their reproductive rights.

The "maternal wall" is constructed around the stereotyped ideas about women's role in the family, which still assumes all responsibility falls on her.

Conclusion

The glass ceiling is a phenomenon affecting the structure of workplaces in contemporary society, that is linked with unfair and stereotyped ideas about women, ethnic minorities, people living with disabilities or sexual minorities, amongst others.

The glass ceiling has a negative effect on those individuals and groups of people as it stops them from advancing in their professional careers.

The barriers that glass ceilings put in place are biased because they are not based on objective factors. Rather, people with similar qualifications or work experience will not be promoted based on prejudice and discrimination.

The term glass ceiling is most often used when discussing limitations for minorities and women in the workplace. These limitations most often include barriers to opportunity, salary increase and promotions.
"You know I hate to say it but I definitely think that there is a glass ceiling for women that disallows them from progressing to the extent of their male counterparts," Nancy Prymak, chemical engineer and packaging manager at Sandoz Pharmaceuticals, said.

Are you an administrative assistant concerned that your job could be replaced by chatbots? It's a worry shared by many in the current digital age. Technology is advancing rapidly, and automation has become increasingly prevalent. But what are the chances of chatbot technology replacing administrative assistants? In this article, we'll explore the risks posed to administrative positions from emerging technologies such as chatbots.

The prevalence of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics have caused much speculation about their potential impact on jobs traditionally held by human workers. Job automation has been used extensively across various work sectors, including finance and healthcare – but could it affect administrative roles? Recent studies suggest there may be cause for concern among those who work in admin-related fields.

Despite these worries, experts agree that AI should not be viewed as a tool to replace humans completely. Rather, they believe that when combined with human input, AI can enhance productivity levels and open up new opportunities for employees in the workplace. This article will discuss both sides of the debate surrounding if/how chatbot technology could disrupt the role of an administrative assistant – so read on!

Definition Of Chatbots

Chatbots are computer programs that communicate with users via text or voice. They use artificial intelligence (AI) to simulate conversations and provide automated responses based on pre-defined rules. Chatbot technology is becoming increasingly popular, as it enables businesses to offer customers a more personalized experience when interacting with their services.

The term "chatbot" was first used in the early 1960s by MIT professor Joseph Weizenbaum. He described them as "an experiment in which computers were programmed to carry out simple dialogues with human beings". Since then, chatbots have evolved significantly and now come in many different forms such as virtual assistants, customer service agents, online shopping bots, and even medical diagnosis systems. As AI continues to develop at an ever-increasing rate, so too does the potential for chatbots to revolutionize how we interact with machines. With this in mind, it's understandable why people might be concerned about the future of their job roles being replaced by chatbots.

History Of Automation In Admin Jobs

It is a valid assumption that automation and technology has been replacing manual labor since the Industrial Revolution. Admin jobs are no exception, as machines have replaced some of the tasks that used to be handled by administrative assistants. Here's a brief overview of how automation in admin roles have evolved over time:

Automation began with typewriters, making it easier for secretaries to type up documents much faster than if they were writing them out by hand.

In the 1980s, computers became commonplace in offices, allowing admin staff to do more complex calculations and file management.

In recent years, advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and chatbot technology have made it possible for automated systems to handle many routine queries from customers – something which was once done exclusively by human administrative assistants.

In light of this history, it does seem likely that there may eventually come a day where certain aspects of an administrative assistant's job could be taken over by AI or chatbots. However, it is also important to note that even with these technological advancements, humans still remain irreplaceable due to their problem solving skills and creativity which cannot yet be replicated by machines.

Current Use Of Automation In Admin Jobs

Automation has become increasingly prevalent in the modern workplace, and administrative jobs are no exception. Technology trends such as artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) have been adopted by companies, allowing for automation to take on more of the workload previously done by admin workers. This has led to many speculating if there is a risk that administrative assistant roles will be replaced by chatbots or other automated processes.

Studies show that job automation can increase productivity, accuracy and efficiency; however, it cannot replace all aspects of an administrative role. Admin tasks require critical thinking skills which machines do not possess, making them unsuited for certain tasks such as problem solving or customer service support. As a result, while some elements of admin roles may be taken over by automation, these positions are unlikely to be eliminated entirely anytime soon.

Advantages And Disadvantages Of Chatbot Technology

Moving on from the current use of automation in admin jobs, it is important to consider the advantages and disadvantages of chatbot technology. Chatbots have become increasingly popular for a number of reasons; they are cost-effective, can handle multiple tasks at once, and require minimal human intervention. Additionally, they can provide 24/7 customer support and respond faster than most humans would be able to. On the other hand, there are some drawbacks associated with using this technology as well. For example, many people find that bots lack empathy or understanding when interacting with customers and clients. They also tend to rely heavily on pre-programmed responses instead of offering personalized help based on individual needs.

Despite these potential downsides, chatbot technology has been shown to be a valuable tool in streamlining administrative processes and providing efficient customer service solutions. As such, it may offer businesses a way to reduce costs while still maintaining high levels of productivity and customer satisfaction. However, it is important for employers to weigh both sides before making any decisions about whether or not to incorporate this type of technology into their workplace operations.

The development of chatbot technology has been a rapidly growing industry in recent years, and it could have an impact on the job market for administrative assistants. Automation is one way that companies are beginning to use this type of technology, which may lead them to choose a machine over a human worker. This could potentially result in some positions becoming redundant or replaced by automated processes. With admin automation being increasingly used, there is certainly potential for jobs like administrative assistant to become obsolete due to advances in AI-powered chatbots.

While these advantages make them attractive options for employers, it means that there is risk of job replacement if more companies adopt this technology. As such, those currently working in the field should consider their options carefully when deciding whether or not to stay in their position.

It's clear that the possibility of job replacement exists within the administrative assistant role given the advancements made in chatbot technology; however, only time will tell how much of an effect this will have on current workers' livelihoods.

While automation and chatbot technology are becoming more commonplace, it is wrong to assume that the role of an administrative assistant will become obsolete. In fact, human resources departments have a tremendous opportunity to leverage this technology in order to improve efficiency within their organizations. Automation can help streamline processes related to recruitment, performance management, payroll and benefits administration, as well as employee engagement initiatives. This would free up time for HR personnel to focus on other strategic activities that require face-to-face collaboration with employees.

Moreover, utilizing automation tools such as chatbots allow companies to respond quickly and accurately to inquiries from both current and potential employees. Companies could use these technologies not only to save money by reducing staffing costs but also gain access to data analytics that provide insights into improving existing policies or creating new ones. Thus, far from replacing administrative assistants, advances in automation give human resources departments the potential to increase productivity while providing valuable services for their organization's workforce.

Challenges Facing Administrative Assistants

Administrative assistants face a number of challenges in their job. One challenge is automation, which can replace many tasks that administrative assistants have traditionally performed. Automation presents a risk for admin assistant job replacement, as chatbots and other automated technologies become more advanced and efficient at handling work-related tasks. This means that an administrative assistant's role could potentially be replaced by technology over time. Additionally, the rise of digital communication has led to increased demands on admin assistants' time, with fewer resources being allocated to help them manage workloads efficiently. As such, it's important for admins to stay up-to-date on the latest tools and trends in order to remain competitive in the workplace. To do this successfully requires regular training and development opportunities in order to keep current skills relevant.

The possibility of job replacement due to advances in automation is one of the most significant challenges facing administrative assistants today. Therefore, developing strong technical abilities will be essential if they are going to remain successful and valuable members of any team or organization. By staying informed about new technological developments, honing existing skillsets through further training, and taking full advantage of available resources, admin assistants can ensure their roles continue to be vital parts of businesses well into the future.

Do you ever worry that your job will be replaced by a chatbot? It's understandable; automation is becoming increasingly prevalent in the modern workplace. Fortunately, there are strategies you can use to mitigate the risk of replacement.

First and foremost, it's important to recognize which tasks could potentially be managed by a chatbot or other automated system. By identifying what processes could be done more efficiently with technology, you can better understand how your role might change over time. Additionally, it pays off to learn about emerging technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI) so you can stay up-to-date on trends related to chatbots and their capabilities.

Make sure you're comfortable using necessary software applications as well as advanced tools such as machine learning algorithms.

Have an understanding of coding languages and data science principles so you have an edge in adapting quickly to new systems if needed.

Attend seminars or workshops offered at tech companies, universities or conferences – this way, you'll stay informed and gain valuable insights into current trends related to automation and job replacement.

By taking these steps, not only will you become a more attractive candidate for potential employers but also help yourself stand out among others who may face similar risks associated with automated systems replacing human workers. Taking proactive measures now will ensure that no matter what changes come down the line, you'll always remain one step ahead – making sure your place in the workforce remains secure!

As technology advances, it is plausible that certain administrative assistant roles may be taken over by chatbots or other automated systems. Retraining programs can help administrators gain new skills such as automation training which involves developing competency with software applications and robotic process automation (RPA). Additionally, they can also learn digital literacy techniques like data analysis, coding, and problem-solving methods. Organizations should invest in providing resources for employees who wish to upgrade their knowledge and stay ahead of the curve when it comes to changing trends in the industry. With all these advantages on offer, there's no reason why any administrative assistant shouldn't take advantage of re-training opportunities available today.

Cost Savings For Businesses Using Automation

As businesses continue to look for ways to cut costs and operate more efficiently, many are turning to automation. From chatbots that provide customer service to automated administrative assistants, the potential cost savings associated with automation is highly attractive.

One example of an organization that has adopted advanced technologies such as robotics, artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning is a large grocery chain in the United States. The company deployed robotic systems designed to autonomously move products from one location in the store to another. This technology reduced manual labor costs by up to 80%. Additionally, AI-based chatbot software was introduced which drastically reduced customer service time allowing employees to be reassigned for other tasks. As a result, this allowed the business to save millions of dollars each year on overhead expenses like payroll and employee wages – making it clear why so many businesses are considering investing in automation solutions.

From improved customer experience and decreased wait times, there's no doubt that automation can offer significant cost savings benefits when implemented correctly. Automation also has the potential to increase efficiency while reducing human error; two factors critical for any successful business today. Companies should carefully consider their options before implementing any type of automation solution but given its impressive track record it's hard not deny how valuable these technologies can be when applied strategically.

Ethical Considerations Surrounding Use Of Automation

The use of automation, such as chatbots, can be beneficial in many ways. However, there are ethical considerations that must be taken into account when using automation to replace humans for certain tasks. One example is the potential replacement of administrative assistants by chatbots. While this could save employers money and allow them to operate more efficiently, it raises an important question: What happens to those who have dedicated their lives and livelihoods to these jobs?

In order to ensure that job replacement due to automation is done ethically, companies should consider providing compensation or other support for those whose jobs may be eliminated. Additionally, they should provide resources and training programs so that employees can learn how to adapt their skillset if needed. This will help mitigate any disruption caused by the influx of automated tools in the workplace while still allowing businesses to take advantage of the benefits offered by new technologies.

Regulations And Compliance Requirements For Use Of Chatbots

The use of chatbots in the workplace is growing. As such, understanding the regulations and compliance requirements for their usage has become increasingly important. In many countries, there are laws relating to automation that need to be taken into account when implementing a chatbot. For example, certain data privacy laws may apply when collecting user information from a chatbot. Other regulatory considerations could include labor standards and anti-discrimination measures.

In addition, employers must ensure any automated system complies with safety guidelines set out by relevant governing bodies or industry associations. The rules vary between jurisdictions but generally involve regular reviews of systems used to identify potential issues or vulnerabilities in the environment where the chatbot is operated from. It's also essential to ensure appropriate security protocols are in place so as not to expose confidential customer data stored within the bot's database.

Chatbots can provide great value but it's critical they're deployed responsibly and compliantly – both internally and externally – if they're being used by a company or organization. Taking all these factors into consideration will help protect an employer's reputation and guard against legal action due to non-compliance with applicable laws and regulations.

Alternatives To Replacing Employees With Automation

It is possible that administrative assistants may be replaced by chatbots in the future. However, there are alternatives to automation which can reduce this risk and help career development. These include:

Career advancement – There are a number of opportunities for administrative assistants to progress their careers beyond the role they currently occupy. With additional training or qualifications, individuals may move into higher positions such as executive assistant, office manager or even supervisor roles.

Job diversification – Administrative assistants could also look to diversify their skillset by taking on other tasks within the organization such as data entry, customer service or marketing support. This would make them more valuable to employers and less likely to be replaced with automation solutions.

Upskilling – Taking courses related to new technologies can help administrative assistants stay ahead of the curve when it comes to job security and ensure they remain relevant in an ever-evolving workplace environment. By making use of these strategies, administrative assistants can put themselves in a better position should automation pose any threat to their job security in the future.

What The Future Holds For Administrative Assistants

So, is there a risk that administrative assistants' jobs will be replaced by chatbots? After evaluating current trends and industry research, it appears that while some tasks may become automated, the role of admin assistants is far from being eliminated.

Automation can help streamline processes, but many companies recognize the need for human support to handle complex customer queries or complete high-level tasks such as data analysis. Admin assistants who have specialized skillsets and understand market dynamics can provide valuable insight on how best to utilize replacement strategies within their organizations. Companies are also beginning to invest more into training programs so that future admin assistants have the necessary tools to succeed in this evolving landscape.

Rather than replacing them altogether, administrators must learn to adapt and evolve alongside new technology if they want to stay competitive in the job market. Those who embrace change and acquire new skills will remain vital members of their organization's success in years to come.

Conclusion

As an administrative assistant, it's important to understand the potential risks of automation replacing your job. While there are many advantages that come with using chatbots and other forms of automation, such as cost savings for businesses, there is still uncertainty over when this technology may become a threat to admin assistant positions.

Despite the growing presence of automation in the workplace however, human employees can remain competitive through continued education and networking opportunities.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is a complex and multifaceted field that involves the development and implementation of algorithms and technologies that enable machines to learn from data and perform tasks that typically require human-level intelligence, such as perception, reasoning, and decision-making. The concept of AI has evolved significantly since the inception of the field in the mid-20th century, with different authors and researchers offering their own perspectives and definitions.

Novitske, L. (2018) viewed AI as a branch of computer science that focuses on developing intelligent machines that can perform tasks that require human-like intelligence. Others view AI as a collection of techniques and methods for building intelligent systems that can learn from data, reason and make decisions based on that data. Still others view AI as a set of tools and technologies that can be used to automate and improve various aspects of human life, from healthcare and education to transportation and entertainment.

Despite these different perspectives, most authors agree that AI is a rapidly advancing field that has the potential to transform many aspects of society and create significant new opportunities and challenges in the years to come. (Congressional Research Service Report, 2020).

Robotics is the interdisciplinary field of science and engineering that deals with the design, construction, operation, and use of robots. Robots are machines that are designed to perform tasks autonomously or semi-autonomously, with or without human intervention. They are typically equipped with sensors, actuators, and computer processors that enable them to sense and interact with the physical environment, as well as process information and make decisions based on that information.

Robotics encompasses many different areas of study, including mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, computer science, and artificial intelligence. It is used in a wide range of applications, such as manufacturing, healthcare, agriculture, space exploration, and entertainment. The goal of robotics is to create machines that can perform tasks that are either too dangerous, too difficult, or too tedious for humans to perform, or to augment human capabilities by providing assistance in tasks that require precision or strength.

The role of a secretary has evolved over time, and modern secretaries are often referred to as administrative assistants or executive assistants. Why is Siri female? When the revolutionary voice assistant launched on iPhones in 2010, her gender was taken as a given in the face of her quick-witted, futuristic abilities. It wasn't until 2017 that male options were provided and by then Microsoft's Cortana (which still doesn't have the option for a male-voiced counterpart) was on the scene as well as Amazon's Alexa. However, it didn't take long for people to push the boundaries of what they could ask ask the new female AIs, prompting Siri to respond to sexual questions or commentary with, "I'd blush if I could." Uncoincidentally, this phrase forms the title of a new United Nations report that examines how female AI voices perpetuate harmful gender stereotypes and what that could mean in the future as they become more integrated into our daily lives.

Culturally, there are already pervasive stereotypes about women being secretaries, assistants, and generally subservient. In addition, market research and even Amazon's own focus groups have shown that consumers associate female voices with being more pleasing and comforting. So, if you're a tech company trying to market a universally appealing virtual helper it's little surprise that a docile, somewhat flirtatious-sounding woman is (consciously or unconsciously) your go-to voice.

Beyond the obvious technical requirements, creating an appealing Siri, Cortana, or Google Home involves teams of software engineers and creative professionals who make a significant effort to create whole backstories and personalities that help the assistant appeal to customers.

"The assistant is, in effect, hardly a generic woman," the U.N. report states, "but rather a young woman from a particular place and shaped by life experiences that carry meaning for the (presumably, mostly American) team that designed 'her' personality and voice."

In Google's case for example, the nameless but distinctively (intentionally) female assistant was, "...imagined as: a young woman from Colorado; the youngest daughter of a research librarian and physics professors who has a B.A. in history from Northwestern, an elite research university in the United States; and as a child, won US $100,000 on Jeopardy Kids Edition," James Giangola, a lead conversation and personality designer for Google Assistant, told The Atlantic.

Many experts, and the U.N. report itself, call out the male-dominated teams that are designing these seemingly innocent backstories. The underrepresentation and absence of women, people of color, and those in the LGBTQ communities in the tech world has been acutely felt in AI and algorithm design, and the lack of diverse perspectives can let conscious and unconscious biases guide the technology's behavior.

"Companies like Apple and Amazon, staffed by overwhelmingly male engineering teams, have built AI systems that cause their feminized digital assistants to greet verbal abuse with catch-me-if-you-can flirtation," the report states. "Because the speech of most voice assistants is female, it sends a signal that women are ... docile and eager-to-please helpers, available at the touch of a button or with a blunt voice command like 'hey' or 'OK'."

This has brought up issues around how to treat AI assistants, particularly when children are beginning to interact with them and give them orders from a young age. Already, consumer responses to voice assistants range from formal and polite to intentionally disrespectful, and in general the expectation has become that all voice assistants will be female.

"If you talk derogatory to an Alexa, children pick this up," Robert LoCascio, CEO of an integrated messaging company called LivePerson, told NPR in an interview. "They go back to school and they think this is the way you talk to someone and this is maybe the way you talk to women."

Solutions to this challenge are, as one might expect, highly complicated. However, the creative studio Virtue Nordic, recently released a genderless AI voice that could go a long way towards solving this problem. The voice is called Q, and its creators tested it with over, "4,600 people identifying as non-binary from Denmark, the U.K., and Venezuela, who rated the voice on a scale of 1 to 5–1 being 'male' and 5 being 'female,'" until they received consistent feedback that the voice was gender-neutral.

While Q wasn't created for any particular tech company, its creators hope that it can influence the conversations being had about gendered AIs and hopefully get picked up as a "third option" for Siri and Alexa.

To their credit, major tech companies have begun making changes to their voice assistants' responses to make them less submissive. According to the report, "Examples of female digital assistants capable of robust defence are harder to find, although recent updates to Apple, Amazon, Google and Microsoft operating systems have eliminated some of the most excessively apologetic or flirtatious responses to sexual harassment."

In addition, these updates have given some voice assistants, Google Home specifically, the ability to interact more positively with users that engage with them using "please" and "thank you."

A World Of Fembots

Why do our most frequently used virtual assistants have female voices to begin with? An Amazon Alexa spokesperson told us that when they tested Alexa, both men and women preferred a female voice. In one Apple ad from 2012 — a few months after Siri launched on the iPhone 4s — Samuel L. Jackson goes through a series of commands, before telling Siri, at the end of the ad, that she can take the night off. Her response is submissive: "If you say so."

"We're basically training our kids that they can bark commands at a female and she will respond," says Ben Parr, the cofounder of chatbot company Octane AI, of our voice-controlled assistants. "

The story of office work is really the story of how a job category was engineered to be feminine, then engineered to stay subordinate even as the tools around it kept changing. Before the Civil War, clerical work in the United States was a male apprenticeship track: clerks worked closely with their bosses, expected promotion into management or ownership, and treated the job as a stepping stone rather than a destination. That began to unravel when the Civil War created a labor shortage that pulled women into government clerking, where they reportedly did "more and better work than men for half the price," and the practice stuck after the war ended. As firms consolidated into large corporations in the late nineteenth century, paperwork volume exploded, clerking splintered into narrow specialized roles, and a middle-management layer rose up to separate owners from a growing mass of low-level workers who no longer had a path upward. The typewriter arrived at exactly this moment, and economic historians argue the causation ran from expanding corporate demand for cheap correspondence labor to the workforce, rather than the machine itself creating the shift: literate white women were available and willing to fill it, since men with equivalent literacy could instead aspire to management. The numbers moved fast: women were roughly 40 percent of typists and stenographers in 1880 and about 95 percent by 1930, with one economic historian putting the female share of all clerical workers at 2.5 percent in 1870 rising to 52.5 percent by 1930. By the 1930s the private secretary had become the emblematic dead-end job: intimate with her boss's work but structurally barred from rising, expected to accept subordination as the price of a position she supposedly held only out of economic need. Automation did not reverse this pattern so much as relabel it: in the postwar office, mainframe computers were sold as eliminators of clerical labor even as the workforce of typists and data-entry clerks kept growing, because "automation" as a term obscured an intensification of human effort behind the mystique of the machine. When the QWERTY keyboard was "neutered" from a feminine to a gender-neutral instrument in the early 1980s, male managers began typing their own correspondence and called it automation rather than an imposition, even as typist positions fell by tens of thousands while the underlying clerical workforce kept expanding overall. Fifty years after computers entered the office, the status quo held remarkably steady: secretarial and administrative work remained the single most common job category for American women from the 1950s through 2010, and full-time women in that role still earned notably less than men in the same title. Frustration with exactly this pattern of invisibility, low pay, and open-ended personal errands drove Karen Nussbaum and Ellen Cassedy, two college-educated Boston secretaries, to found 9to5 in 1973, choosing a name that signaled a demand for defined hours and fair treatment rather than being at a boss's constant disposal. The organization's early tactics combined muckraking with humor, exposing an illegal Boston employer wage-fixing scheme that led to pay raises of 10 percent or more and later running "worst boss" contests, before growing into chapters nationwide and eventually forming a union affiliated with the Service Employees International Union. In the 1980s 9to5 specifically studied how the arrival of office computers was affecting the secretarial workforce and pregnancy-related workplace hazards, treating the technology itself as a labor issue rather than an inevitability to be simply absorbed. The glass ceiling entered the vocabulary around the same period, credited by some to a 1978 panel discussion where consultant Marilyn Loden argued that cultural rather than personal barriers held women back, and popularized soon after by a Wall Street Journal description of invisible barriers to the top of corporate hierarchies. A federal commission convened in the 1990s identified societal, internal-structural, and governmental barriers behind the glass ceiling, and by 1995 men still held 95 percent of management positions even though women held nearly half of all jobs, a gap that legislation from the Equal Pay Act through the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act only partially closed. A 9to5 organizer later captured the residual problem precisely: the glass ceiling is cracking in different places, but a "sticky floor" keeps most women concentrated in traditionally female jobs like administrative support in the first place, so cracking the ceiling for a few does little for the many stuck below it. That sticky floor is exactly where AI is now landing hardest: a Revelio Labs analysis found that AI-threatened occupations are disproportionately held by women because women remain concentrated in roles like administrative assistants, executive secretaries, and payroll clerks, with IBM's CEO projecting up to 30 percent of comparable back-office roles could be automated within five years. One widely cited automation-risk estimate put secretaries and assistants at 96 percent likelihood of displacement, on par with cashiers and office clerks, though risk is not uniform across all women, since a McKinsey analysis found Black women face lower automation-driven job-loss risk than Black men or than white and Asian workers of either gender. The gendering has not stayed confined to human job titles either: consumer AI assistants like Siri, Cortana, and Alexa were built with feminized personas, and researchers connect this design choice directly to the long history of the secretary as a feminized, always-available support function, itself echoed by a workforce in which women remain a small minority of AI researchers and conference authors. Put together, the history suggests a durable pattern worth naming rather than assuming has been solved: each new office technology, from the typewriter through the mainframe to generative AI, has been introduced with promises of liberating workers, yet has tended to intensify or relabel women's labor rather than upgrade its status or pay, while those designing and deploying it remain disproportionately male. The lessons from 9to5 and the glass-ceiling fight point toward the same practical takeaway today: naming and quantifying the problem, organizing collectively around concrete pay and workload data, and treating "who designs and who absorbs the new technology" as a governance question have historically moved the needle more than hoping status will rise automatically as tools improve.

{"query": "feminization of clerical work history male clerks female typists secretaries", "k": 10, "results": [{"rank": 1, "id": "shard_01710_72297", "docid": "shard_01710_72297", "kind": "document", "rrf_score": 0.032266, "text": "A Woman's Place is at the Typewriter

Contents

Margery Davies is currently the Director of Diversity Education and Development at Tufts University. She holds a Ph.D. in Sociology from Brandeis University.nhghnghn

Woman's Place is at the Typewriter: Office Work and Office Workers 1870-1930Edit

In this text, Davies writes an intensive history of clerical labor. For Davies, this period contains the most striking changes in clerical labor—it spans the shift from primarily male to primarily female labor. The clerical work environment that existed by 1930 is still, more or less, the organizational system that exists today. The major shift was in class and gender. Prior to the civil war, clerical work was a male dominated field in which males worked closely with their superiors and were often apprenticed to them; their superiors success was their success, and they could look forward to a position of management and business ownership in their later years. By 1930, however, clerical workers were a secretarial proletariat—subordinate to her superiors, with no opportunity for advancement.

Clerical work in this period was largely done by banks, lawyers offices and businesses. They handwrote [as copyists or scriveners] documents in multiple, to be dispensed to the appropriate parties. Their primary skill was penmanship, as was copyediting. However, few places employed dedicated copyists (lawyers or large merchants). Usually not enough paperwork existed to solely occupy a copyist. Instead, there were clerks, whose work included composition, book-keeping, debt collecting, copying etc. There did not exist standards in copy work or book keeping. Beneath them was the errand boy who kept house and gathered supplies, etc., and he would one day be a clerk. Chains of command were straightfoward, and there was a high degree of internal trust based on the personal nature of apprenticeship. Upward mobility was likely, and for those who would not rise to ownership, they were valued and trusted office managers. The clerk class was more akin to management than what it would become after the Civil War.

The shape and scale of business drastically change in the closing decades of the 19th century. Smaller, competitive firms became swallowed up by vertically and horizontally integrated corporations, and trusts helped facilitate this movement. The volume of business increased, requiring more dedicated attention to book and record keeping—memory no longer sufficed. Records were also employed to prevent fraud. As work expanded, the simple jobs of clerk, book-keeper, copyist and errand boy exploded into different types of semi-skilled clerks—shipping clerks, billing clerks, file clerks, etc. Tasks became more specialized and certain roles only performed that role. In general, middle management arose as firms became too large to be personally managed by the owners. Lower-end workers no longer had direct access to viewing the function of a business, to "learning the business on the job". This also generates the tension between owners and employees concerning labor hours and work week, until they are eventually shortened in the 1930s to 5 days a week and something close to an 8 hour work day.

With the typewriter, positions for stenographers and typists emerged. A stenographer might take dictation and transcribe a letter, and then pass it to a gang of typists for bulk reproduction.

Typewriters were slow to catch on. In 1874, James Densmore went to great lengths to promote the design of Christopher Sholes. After producing a batch a no profit, he got Remington (the gun maker) to produce 1000 of them, and then tried to sell them in Manhattan from $125 each. Only 400 sold. In the 1870s, typewriters were still full of kinks and typing was considered poor etiquette. By the 1880s, however, demand soared, with multiple companies producing 15000 a year. In this sense, the typewriter "followed in the wake of basic alterations in capitalism" (38). Faster than handwriting, it allowed for duplication and processing at higher speed. While it did facilitate the entrance of women in the workplace, capitalism was moreso responsible for this. Typewriters did facilitate more rigorous hierarchies at work and diminished upward mobility; it required the labor of a skilled typist, and typists were only trained to type, so they lacked options for higher levels of employment.

By most accounts, female clerical workers were white native women, in better employment situations than their industrial-laboring counterparts (see Wage-Earning Women). While their wages were not high, they're working conditions were at least favorable. However, Davies does argue that female clerical workers worked because they had to, not to garner "pin money" (77). A girl was expected to contribute to her own support (presumably while living at home during the years between school and marriage).

Female entrance into the workforce began during the Civil War, when soldiering caused a labor shortage. Women were hired as government clerks, and kept after the war—it was reported they did more and better work than men for half the price. The overall feminization of the workforce proceeded briskly from the 1870s onward. In 1880 women were 40% of typists and stenographers, and 95% by 1930 (not true in all cases—lesser stats in bookkeeping and accountancy, and almost nothing as messengers). Work as a typist or stenographer had never been understood as "men's work" and thus there were few barriers for entrance. However, Davies insists the typewriter was not responsible for women entering the workplace any more than it was responsible for the expansion of the office. Rather, firms expanded and consolidated after the Civil War, requiring higher quantities of correspondence. It was the expansion of the office that called for high volumes of semi-skilled, inexpensive laborers with little ambition for upward mobility—jobs most easily filled by native, literate white women. Men took the positions of managerial importance that were created by this boom—which is exactly why they didn't look for work as typists: "A man who had enough education and literacy skills (the ability to spell reasonably well, to write a legible hand, to do basic arithmetic accurately) to obtain a job as a clerical worker was also probably educated enough to at least aspire to, and in many cases to attain, a managerial or professional position" (57). Women were graduating from high school in higher numbers than men, while men graduated college in higher numbers than women. Thus, men with literacy skills typically pursued college and entered managerial positions, while women with basic literacy skills and diplomas were ready for clerical work. Additionally, the re-organization of labor facilitated female entrance, dispelling taboos around women and offering new titles unattached to gender roles.

Women were available for these jobs for a variety of reasons. The decline of small family farms, industrial work was onerous and humiliating, small family business was unstable, the home was no longer a site of goods production (which for Davies means more opportunities outside the home, but Cowan comes to a different conclusion in More Work for Mother), and clerical work was one of the only sites available to literate women.

Scientific management pursued transforming the office (much like the assembly line) into a place of efficiency. Mundane tasks were distributed to the least paid, so that more specialized labor could be gleened from a semi-skilled employee. Hand movements were managed, as well as desk arrangements to diminish distraction.

Davies ends with a chapter on the private secretary—the perfect dead-end job for a woman working only out of economic necessity. Scientific management controlled little of her routine. The private secretary was almost predominantly female by the 1930s, and maintained a personal (but no longer upwardly mobile) relationship with her superior. In essence, the private secretary and her manager shared one job—she only took care of the menial tasks. Because they were isolated from other office workers, they did not identify with their labor position. However, feminization of this position reinforced its subordinate position, and she should not resent the power and control of the male (whereas a male secretary might), as they would never aspire to a higher position.", "truncated": false, "original_chars": 8425, "returned_chars": 8425}, {"rank": 2, "id": "shard_00041_9455", "docid": "shard_00041_9455", "kind": "document", "rrf_score": 0.030366, "text": "With the neutering of the QWERTY keyboard in the early 1980s following largely successful clerical worker organizing, male workers in offices began taking on clerical work that, until recently, they would have considered beneath both their job descriptions and their manhood. Paradoxically, the men who now began typing, filing, and performing data entry for themselves did not generally consider the imposition of these new tasks an increase in work. Rather, they called it “automation.” Employers’ and computer manufacturers’ regendering of the QWERTY keyboard from feminine to neuter in the last quarter of the twentieth century was an example of the uses and power of the automation discourse, an ideological commitment that obscured the intensification of human labor behind utopian rhetoric and technological enthusiasm. Employers regendered the keyboard to get more work out of their employees, and as they did so, they claimed that no one did the work at all. Obscuring human labor behind technological marvels, the claims that the work was done by “automation” proved persuasive, even as human labor was sped up and intensified.
For most of its history, the alphanumeric keyboard was a feminine instrument. When engineers in the early 1970s built a computer system for the personal use of Chilean president Salvador Allende, they installed no keyboards; they did not wish to humiliate the president by likening him to an office “girl.” Instead, the president was to summon information by pressing any of a number of blank, geometrically idealized buttons: a pentagon, a square, a circle. For his part, science fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke found it easier to imagine colonies on the moon than an unsexed keyboard. In his 1961 novel, A Fall of Moondust, Clarke gendered a fictional computer that automatically transformed speech into typed pages (an “Electrosecretary”) as female. “All Electrosecs,” he wrote, “were ‘she.’ ”1
Masculine exceptions to the keyboard's femininity were made where the work was considered highly skilled or craft-like: the newsman typing an article; Hemingway at his Underwood; and, later in the century, the computer programmer coding late into the night. The masculine trades aside, however, proximity to the keyboard almost always indicated a worker's low status and, often, their sex. Having entered the office in the late nineteenth century under a masculine sign, by the first decades of the twentieth century the QWERTY keyboard's association with degraded female office labor meant that no self-respecting executive or midlevel manager—whose ranks were for the most part closed to women—would, except in extreme circumstances, operate a keyboard. The keyboard was the province of secretaries and low-wage clerical workers, almost all of whom were women.
By the end of the century, however, all of this had changed. In the early 1980s the alphanumeric keyboard made a sudden and almost complete transition from a feminine to a neuter device. No longer would QWERTY spell “female.” With a gender-neutral keyboard, middle managers could shoulder the labor of clerical workers—that is, the labor of “girls”—and still consider themselves men. They could type, file, and enter data, tasks that only a few years earlier they would have seen as beneath both their paygrade and their dignity. When married to a computer, or so the ad men insisted, the keyboard was nothing for which a manager need feel ashamed. Ever since executives in the American automobile industry coined the word automation in the years immediately following the Second World War, the term's precise meaning has been the subject of intense debate. “There is much truth in the quip,” said one of the word's earliest and most successful promoters, “that it is as hard for a group of businessmen to define automation as it is for a group of theologians to define sin.”5 This difficulty has been true for historians as well. Nussbaum later served as the director of the Department of Labor's Women's Bureau during the first Clinton administration, and is the founding director of Working America, the largest non-union workers' group in the U.S.
How the movement started
9to5 focused on improving pay and working conditions for women around the country. But at the beginning, it was the feeling of being invisible as a woman office worker that propelled the Nussbaum and 9to5 co-founder Ellen Cassedy into action.
"[It was] the notion that somehow we were expendable, not important, not even worthy of knowing our names very often," Nussbaum said in an interview with "Marketplace Morning Report" host David Brancaccio. "We had members of the organization who said their bosses couldn't keep them straight when there were two women in the office."
It was only when the organizers looked into the data that they realized that women clerical workers, many of whom held college degrees, generally earned less than factory workers.
Activists attend a 9to5 meeting. (Richard Bermack)
Nussbaum and Cassedy started in Boston, distributing a newsletter to secretaries around town and holding meetings at the local YWCA. They started organizing around issues like low pay, harassment and nonexistent job descriptions that left them doing personal errands for men in their offices.

Glass Ceiling Definition

The glass ceiling refers both to impediments and invisible barriers that women, ethnic minorities, and other groups, such as disabled or gay people, encounter in the workplace and that stop them from advancing professionally past a certain point.

The term was coined in 1978 by Marylin Loden, a managerial consultant in a Telecoms company in the US who was taking part in a panel discussion about women's aspirations.

Marylin argued that it was cultural barriers (the "invisible glass ceiling") not personal ones that stopped women from advancing in their careers.

The glass ceiling can be found in all domains and in all types of organizations, whether public or private. The barriers are thought of as invisible because they are not defined corporate policies, but rather norms or implicit biases that are accepted.

Barriers may be a result of unconscious bias or prejudice, which overlook a person's qualifications or achievements and stops them from being promoted.

Breaking the glass ceiling is a difficult task, and doing it means overcoming all the barriers and obstacles that are put on the way. The importance of breaking the glass ceiling lies in that it can help remove barriers for others who are in a similar position.

First Female Leader of the Fortune 500: The Fortune 500 CEO glass ceiling was broken by Katharine Graham in 1963 when she became CEO of the Washington Post.

Female Vice Presidents: Just as there has been a lack of female presidents, we can see that there is also a historical lack of female vice presidents. Kamala Harris was the first.

Causes of the Glass Ceiling

Discrimination against potential mothers: Women who are entering an age where they may have children may not be offered promotions at the workplace, while paternity is not contemplated amongst men of the same birth cohort.

People from ethnic minority backgrounds are sometimes left behind in their careers due to discriminatory hiring practices in the workplace.

Gender stereotypes: Sexist stereotypes, for example, thinking of women as more emotional and unable to fulfill leadership roles, contribute to the perpetuation of the glass ceiling

Exclusion from informal networks: Women are often locked out from "informal networks", for example, going for afterwork drinks with managers, which puts them at a disadvantage in career advancement.

The gay glass ceiling: Homosexual men's careers also feel the impact of glass ceilings as research has found they are often concentrated in low-level managerial positions, not at the top (Aksoy et al., 2019).

Discrimination against gay people: People with disabilities have been found to have difficulties both entering the job market and then advancing in their careers once they have secured a job.

Intersectional discrimination: Ethnic minority women often suffer double discrimination when it comes to workplace promotion, and may find it harder to shatter the glass ceiling.

Unnoticed effort: Women trying harder at their job by, for example, trying to make their ideas stand up as a meeting, is also an example of the effects of the glass ceiling (Chisholm-Burns et al., 2017).

Motherhood as a barrier: Motherhood often penalizes women when it comes to advancing in their careers, while it is not the same for fathers, who keep on climbing their professional career.

Attempts to Address the Glass Ceiling

The debate over how to address the glass ceiling generally revolves around how aggressively governments or corporations should intervene to achieve equality of representation.

Below are some common solutions and the arguments for and against each.

1. Affirmative Action

Affirmative action refers to policies to intentionally hire or preference underrepresented groups. On a macro scale, this gets underrepresented people into positions of power and helps achieve political and sociological goals.

However, critics argue that it restrains hiring committees and may lead to worse performance. If the best candidate is a male, for example, then the company should have the freedom to choose the male candidate.

Furthermore, this policy may instill a sense that women only got the job because of their gender identity. To challenge this point, however, we could argue that historically men have only gotten leadership positions because of their gender identities, too.

2. Quotas

Like affirmative action, quotas are used to put pressure on an organization to hire underrepresented groups.

An example of a quota might be "to ensure 60% of new hires are women." This allows a hiring committee to split the hiring pool – so, for example, they can hire 4 men and 6 women in a hiring round when they hire 10 people.

In politics, it might mean that a party will decide that 50% of their candidates will be women in the next election. one complaint about this, however, has been that the parties will run women in regions where they will definitely lose, and run men in the more desirable or competitive races, leading to more men getting elected in the end.

3. Scholarships and Internships

A less coercive policy is to offer scholarships and internships to underrepresented groups.

This approach aims to give people from underrepresented groups the best chance possible to succeed in interviews, without actually forcing the hand of the interviewers.

The criticism of this policy is that it doesn't do anything to tangibly address implicit biases that hiring committees have that will lead them to hiring male or racial majority candidates, even if the female or minority candidates are better.

Research and Case Studies

1. Gender Research

The2. Sexual Orientation Research

Research conducted in the UK showed that gay men were more likely to be in managerial positions or have supervisory responsibilities than heterosexual similar men (Giray Aksoy et al., 2019).

However, a more detailed look showed that the managerial positions held were at the lower level of the scale. The highest level managerial positions were harder to reach for gay men than otherwise similar heterosexual men.

For lesbians, the results were similar. While compared to heterosexual women, lesbians were more likely to have managerial authority, but like gay men, they were less likely to be in the highest managerial or supervisory roles.

There was evidence related to discriminatory practices and also of intersectionality: what has been called the "gay glass ceiling effect" was stronger for ethnic minorities than for whites.

3. Disability Research

The glass ceiling, its obstacles, and barriers also affect the work life of people living with disabilities (Nario-Redmond, 2019). A mix of organizational and attitudinal barriers makes it harder for people with disabilities to advance in their careers.

Research has shown that people with disabilities are still concentrated and over-represented in lower-paid service jobs (Nario-Redmond, 2019; Wilson-Kovacsa et al., 2008). However, in higher-paid managerial and professional positions, they are under-represented.

This situation happens despite the fact that people with disabilities often have equivalent qualifications and work experience as non-disabled work colleagues. And still, they have less opportunities of upward mobility, meaning that the glass ceiling is on full force.

4. Race and Ethnicity Research

Ethnic and racial minorities also see their career advancement halted by the existence of a glass ceiling (Gee & Peck, 2018).

Studies from the US show, for example, that race is a stronger factor than gender in determining a person's chances of being promoted or holding higher managerial positions (Gee & Peck, 2018). This points at the importance of intersectionality when thinking about the glass ceiling (Bloch et al., 2020).

Also, not all ethnic minorities have the same trajectories. In the US context Asians, for example, may be more likely to be hired, but the least likely to be promoted. This has come to be called "the bamboo ceiling" (Yu, 2020).

5. The Maternal Wall Research

Women of childbearing age, pregnant women and those with children are all subjected to the effects of the glass ceiling (Williams, 2015).

Motherhood, or its prospect, seems to be a factor in determining women's career projections and advancements. Fatherhood, however, does not affect men's professional lives in the same manner, pointing at gender bias and inequality.

What has come to be called the "maternal wall", is a situation in which women do not even reach the "glass ceiling" due to a type of gender bias related to their reproductive rights.

The "maternal wall" is constructed around the stereotyped ideas about women's role in the family, which still assumes all responsibility falls on her.

Conclusion

The glass ceiling is a phenomenon affecting the structure of workplaces in contemporary society, that is linked with unfair and stereotyped ideas about women, ethnic minorities, people living with disabilities or sexual minorities, amongst others.

The glass ceiling has a negative effect on those individuals and groups of people as it stops them from advancing in their professional careers.

The barriers that glass ceilings put in place are biased because they are not based on objective factors. Rather, people with similar qualifications or work experience will not be promoted based on prejudice and discrimination.

The story of office work is really the story of how a job category was engineered to be feminine, then engineered to stay subordinate even as the tools around it kept changing.

Before the Civil War, clerical work in the United States and Britain was a male apprenticeship track: clerks worked closely with their bosses, expected promotion into management or ownership, and treated the job as a stepping stone rather than a destination.

That began to unravel when the Civil War created a labor shortage that pulled women into government clerking, where they reportedly did "more and better work than men for half the price," and the practice stuck after the war ended.

As firms consolidated into large vertically integrated corporations in the late nineteenth century, paperwork volume exploded, clerking splintered into narrow specialized roles, and a middle-management layer rose up to separate owners from a growing mass of low-level workers who no longer had a path upward.

The typewriter arrived at exactly this moment, and while it is tempting to credit the machine itself with feminizing the office, the economic historian Claudia Goldin and others argue the causation ran the other way: expanding corporate demand for cheap, semi-skilled correspondence labor called into being a workforce, and literate white women were the ones available and willing to fill it, since men with equivalent literacy could aspire to management instead. [shard_01710_72297]

The numbers moved fast: women were roughly 40 percent of typists and stenographers in 1880 and about 95 percent by 1930 in the United States, with one economic historian putting the share of women among all clerical workers at 2.5 percent in 1870 rising to 52.5 percent by 1930. [shard_01710_72297] [shard_03115_73252]

This was not simply a natural sorting by aptitude; research on clerks in twentieth-century Cape Town shows that where clerical work feminized, it often also became racially exclusive, with legal and social barriers pushing coloured men and women out even as white women moved in, suggesting that patriarchal and racial hierarchies together decided who got which jobs as technology reshaped the office. [shard_03938_61414]

By the 1930s the private secretary had become the emblematic dead-end job: intimate with her boss's work but structurally barred from rising, expected to accept subordination as the price of a position she supposedly only held out of economic need rather than ambition. [shard_01710_72297]

Automation and computerization did not reverse this pattern so much as relabel it: in the postwar office, mainframe computers were sold as eliminators of clerical labor even as the workforce of typists, keypunch operators, and data-entry clerks kept growing, because "automation" as a term obscured an intensification of human effort behind the mystique of the machine. [shard_00041_9455]

When the QWERTY keyboard was "neutered" from a feminine to a gender-neutral instrument in the early 1980s, male managers began typing their own correspondence and called it automation rather than an imposition, even as typist positions fell by tens of thousands and the underlying clerical workforce kept expanding overall. [shard_00041_9455]

Fifty years after the first computers entered offices, the status quo held remarkably steady: secretarial and administrative work remained the single most common job category for American women from the 1950s through 2010, and full-time women in that role still earned notably less than men in the same title. [shard_05856_20348]

Frustration with exactly this pattern of invisibility, low pay, and open-ended personal errands is what drove Karen Nussbaum and Ellen Cassedy, two college-educated Boston secretaries, to found 9to5 in 1973, choosing a name that signaled a demand for defined hours and fair treatment rather than being at a boss's constant disposal. [shard_01041_64296] [shard_02116_79751]

The organization's early tactics combined muckraking with humor, exposing an illegal Boston employer wage-fixing scheme that led to pay raises of 10 percent or more, and later running "worst boss" contests to publicize harassment and demeaning treatment, before growing into chapters nationwide and eventually forming a union affiliated with the Service Employees International Union. [shard_01041_64296] [shard_04003_3903]

In the 1980s 9to5 specifically studied how the arrival of office computers was affecting the secretarial workforce and pregnancy-related workplace hazards, treating the technology itself as a labor issue rather than an inevitability to be simply absorbed. [shard_02116_79751]

The glass ceiling entered the vocabulary around the same period, credited by some to a 1978 panel discussion where consultant Marilyn Loden argued that cultural rather than personal barriers held women back, and popularized by a Wall Street Journal article in the late 1980s describing invisible barriers to the top of corporate hierarchies. A federal commission convened in the 1990s identified societal, internal-structural, and governmental barriers behind the glass ceiling, and by 1995 men still held 95 percent of management positions even though women held nearly half of all jobs, a gap that legislation from the Equal Pay Act through the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act only partially closed. Now I have full committed evidence across all coverage areas: the feminization of clerical work, automation/computerization and status, the 9to5 movement, glass-ceiling debates, and the contemporary AI parallel. I'll write the final report.

The story of office work is really the story of how a job category was engineered to be feminine, then engineered to stay subordinate even as the tools around it kept changing.

Before the Civil War, clerical work in the United States was a male apprenticeship track: clerks worked closely with their bosses, expected promotion into management or ownership, and treated the job as a stepping stone rather than a destination. [shard_01710_72297]

That began to unravel when the Civil War created a labor shortage that pulled women into government clerking, where they reportedly did "more and better work than men for half the price," and the practice stuck after the war ended. [shard_01710_72297]

As firms consolidated into large corporations in the late nineteenth century, paperwork volume exploded, clerking splintered into narrow specialized roles, and a middle-management layer rose up to separate owners from a growing mass of low-level workers who no longer had a path upward. [shard_01710_72297]

The typewriter arrived at exactly this moment, and economic historians argue the causation ran from expanding corporate demand for cheap correspondence labor to the workforce, rather than the machine itself creating the shift: literate white women were available and willing to fill it, since men with equivalent literacy could instead aspire to management. [shard_01710_72297]

The numbers moved fast: women were roughly 40 percent of typists and stenographers in 1880 and about 95 percent by 1930, with one economic historian putting the female share of all clerical workers at 2.5 percent in 1870 rising to 52.5 percent by 1930. [shard_01710_72297] [shard_03115_73252]

This was not simply a natural sorting by aptitude; research on clerks in twentieth-century Cape Town shows that where clerical work feminized it also became racially exclusive, with legal barriers pushing coloured men and women out even as white women moved in, suggesting patriarchal and racial hierarchies together decided who got which jobs as technology reshaped the office. [shard_03938_61414]

By the 1930s the private secretary had become the emblematic dead-end job: intimate with her boss's work but structurally barred from rising, expected to accept subordination as the price of a position she supposedly held only out of economic need rather than ambition. [shard_01710_72297]

Automation did not reverse this pattern so much as relabel it: in the postwar office, mainframe computers were sold as eliminators of clerical labor even as the workforce of typists and data-entry clerks kept growing, because "automation" as a term obscured an intensification of human effort behind the mystique of the machine. [shard_00041_9455]

When the QWERTY keyboard was "neutered" from a feminine to a gender-neutral instrument in the early 1980s, male managers began typing their own correspondence and called it automation rather than an imposition, even as typist positions fell by tens of thousands while the underlying clerical workforce kept expanding overall. [shard_00041_9455]

Even earlier, Civil War widows were hired at Harvard as human "computers" to process astronomical data for low pay and no advancement, a group astronomer Edward Pickering's contemporaries nicknamed "Pickering's Harem," and IBM's 1957 film Desk Set was explicitly designed to reassure office women that a new supercomputer would join their team rather than replace them. [shard_04864_40333]

Fifty years after computers entered the office, the status quo held remarkably steady: secretarial and administrative work remained the single most common job category for American women from the 1950s through 2010, and full-time women in that role still earned notably less than men in the same title. [shard_05856_20348]

Frustration with exactly this pattern of invisibility, low pay, and open-ended personal errands drove Karen Nussbaum and Ellen Cassedy, two college-educated Boston secretaries, to found 9to5 in 1973, choosing a name that signaled a demand for defined hours and fair treatment rather than being at a boss's constant disposal. [shard_01041_64296] [shard_02116_79751]

The organization's early tactics combined muckraking with humor, exposing an illegal Boston employer wage-fixing scheme that led to pay raises of 10 percent or more and later running "worst boss" contests, before growing into chapters nationwide and eventually forming a union affiliated with the Service Employees International Union. [shard_01041_64296] [shard_04003_3903]

In the 1980s 9to5 specifically studied how the arrival of office computers was affecting the secretarial workforce and pregnancy-related workplace hazards, treating the technology itself as a labor issue rather than an inevitability to be simply absorbed. [shard_02116_79751]

The glass ceiling entered the vocabulary around the same period, credited by some to a 1978 panel discussion where consultant Marilyn Loden argued that cultural rather than personal barriers held women back, and popularized by a Wall Street Journal description of invisible barriers to the top of corporate hierarchies. [shard_02866_15955] [shard_00899_51032]

A federal commission convened in the 1990s identified societal, internal-structural, and governmental barriers behind the glass ceiling, and by 1995 men still held 95 percent of management positions even though women held nearly half of all jobs, a gap that legislation from the Equal Pay Act through the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act only partially closed. [shard_00899_51032]

A 9to5 organizer later captured the residual problem precisely: the glass ceiling is cracking in different places, but a "sticky floor" keeps most women concentrated in traditionally female jobs like administrative support in the first place, so cracking the ceiling for a few does little for the many stuck below it. [shard_05856_20348]

That sticky floor is exactly where AI is now landing hardest: a Revelio Labs analysis found that AI-threatened occupations are disproportionately held by women because women remain concentrated in roles like administrative assistants, executive secretaries, and payroll clerks, with IBM's CEO projecting up to 30 percent of comparable back-office roles could be automated within five years. The gendering has not stayed confined to human job titles either: consumer AI assistants like Siri, Cortana, and Alexa were built with feminized personas and voices explicitly because designers found people respond as more comfortable and accepting toward a female voice, and researchers connect this design choice directly to the long history of the secretary as a feminized, always-available support function. [shard_04737_48139] [shard_04864_40333]

That imbalance is compounded by who builds the technology: a UNESCO-linked report found women made up only about 18 percent of authors at AI conferences and under 20 percent of AI professors, with some estimates putting the female share of AI job applicants in Silicon Valley below 1 percent.
